title: Exploring AI-Generated Text in Student Writing: How Does AI Help?
extended_summary:
This paper examines how AI-generated text contributes to secondary school English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) students’ story writing. The core question is not whether AI can write for students, but how students actually use AI-generated text inside their own compositions and whether different patterns of use are associated with better human-rated writing quality. The authors frame the work as human-AI collaborative writing, or “machine-in-the-loop,” where students retain full agency and may choose whether and how to incorporate AI outputs.

The intervention involved two workshops in which students from two Hong Kong secondary schools first learned to build simple AI natural language generation tools using Python, Gradio, Hugging Face, and open-source language models, and then used those tools to write short stories. Students had 45 minutes in the second workshop to write with AI support, using prompting and editing strategies, and later could complete stories for submission to a contest. The analyzed dataset consisted of 23 stories under 500 words, with students marking which text was their own and which was AI-generated. Researchers then analyzed counts and types of AI-generated text, and experts scored each story on content, language, and organization.

The population was 23 Hong Kong secondary school students from two schools serving students with different prior academic achievement levels. The context was EFL creative writing in school workshops rather than a controlled experiment. Quantitative analyses included descriptive statistics, multiple linear regression, and cluster analysis to identify learner profiles based on writing quality and AI usage patterns.

The main conclusion is that both human-written word count and AI-generated word count were significantly associated with higher writing scores, but benefits depended strongly on student competence and strategy. More proficient writers generally relied less on AI yet used it more effectively through editing and selective integration. Some lower-performing students appeared to benefit somewhat, especially in language quality, but heavy AI use did not guarantee strong writing and did not erase underlying differences in writing ability. The authors argue for differentiated pedagogy: stronger writers may benefit from fine-grained instruction in prompting and revision, while weaker writers need more foundational writing support alongside guidance in using AI text strategically.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small, single-group correlational study of secondary students with expert scoring and regression/cluster analyses, but no control group, randomization, or causal identification. It provides direct K-12 evidence, yet credibility is limited by the very small sample and observational design.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests potentially beneficial but inconsistent effects of AI-generated text on writing quality, with no standardized effect size and substantial heterogeneity across students. Impact is therefore unclear rather than convincingly positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: Secondary EFL students used self-built AI natural language generation writing tools to generate editable story text and integrate AI-produced passages into short-story compositions during a machine-in-the-loop writing task.

finding.finding_summary: In a sample of 23 Hong Kong secondary school students, both the number of human-written words and AI-generated words were significantly positively associated with expert-rated writing quality in stories written with AI support. Multiple linear regression showed strong partial correlations between human words and writing scores (Content r_partial=0.937, Language=0.914, Organization=0.943, CLO total=0.951) and moderate positive partial correlations for AI words (Content=0.49, Language=0.537, Organization=0.532, CLO total=0.586), but cluster analyses showed that high AI use did not reliably produce strong writing; some heavy AI users scored highly while others produced short, incomplete, low-scoring stories.
finding.measure: Expert-rated EFL story-writing quality using rubric scores for content, language, organization, CLO total, plus counts of AI-generated words/chunks and total story length
finding.std_deviation: Grand total SD=5.94; CLO SD=4.74; AI words SD=90.56; human words SD=164.69
